## Summary

The austral was launched in 1985 as the new, strong unit of the *Plan Austral* and was briefly worth more than a dollar. Deficits came back, and by 1989 Argentina was in hyperinflation: **197 % in July 1989, doubling every 19.4 days** (H&K). President Alfonsín handed power to Carlos Menem months early. Two more waves followed before the **Convertibility Plan** of 1991 fixed 10,000 australes to the dollar by law; a year later the new peso replaced the austral.

## Causes

- **The debt crisis** of the 1980s: no external credit, capital flight to the dollar.
- **Repeated plans that froze prices without fixing the budget** (Plan Austral 1985, Plan Primavera
  1988); each freeze ended in a bigger jump.

## Timeline

- **15 Jun 1985** — Plan Austral: the austral replaces the peso argentino at 1,000 : 1.
- **Jul 1989** — peak: 197 % (H&K).
- **Mar 1990** — the H&K episode ends.
- **1 Jan 1992** — the peso replaces the austral at 10,000 : 1.

## The end

Convertibility was a quasi-currency-board: no peso could be issued without a dollar in reserve, so the central bank could no longer finance the state. The cure became the next crisis when the peg broke in 2001–02.

## Lessons

- A new currency name without a budget fix (austral 1985) buys about two years.
- A hard anchor works as long as the fiscal side honours it — and fails just as hard when it doesn't.
